title: Mechowodt Treaty and Reserved Rights Landscape, 1639
summary: A 1639 Dutch agreement associated with Mechowodt of the Massapequa/Marossepinck world describes Native people reserving rights to remain on the land, plant corn, fish, hunt, and make a living there.
address_label: South shore landscape, Rockaway-to-Suffolk treaty context
ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as part of a broader south shore diplomatic and land-rights context involving overlapping Native polities.
why_this_matters: The Mechowodt agreement complicates simple stories of land "sale." It shows Native leaders negotiating continued use and presence, and it helps explain how colonial legal records could both preserve Native claims and become instruments of dispossession.
introduction_title: Reserved Rights in a Colonial Record
introduction_content: The Freeport/Merrick south shore helps explain a broad legal landscape and the difference between Native land-use rights and colonial ownership claims.1
history_content:
The rights written into the agreement

The January 15, 1639 record names Mechowodt and other co-owners, including his cousin Piscamoc. Although its transfer language favors the Dutch West India Company, it expressly allows Mechowodt, his people, and friends to remain, plant corn, fish, hunt, and make a living on the land. These were practical conditions for maintaining everyday life.1

The document was recorded at Fort Amsterdam and concerns a broad landscape. Its terms place continuing Native residence and use inside the written agreement itself. Later Hempstead and Mercock land dispute records show Native representatives continuing to contest what colonial possession meant. Reading the agreements together reveals a long negotiation over land and authority, rather than a single moment when Native history ended.12
